scene.testo: Who ordered the invasion of the Soviet Union? At Nuremberg, the Field Marshal who signed the paperwork gave a short answer: one name, Hitler. Then the court heard why that answer saved no one.
Here is the question the Allied prosecutors kept putting to the men in the dock. Who gave the order for Operation Barbarossa, and who carried it out? One defendant knew the answer better than anyone.
But the real weight of the answer is not the name. It is what the court did with it, and what it cost the man who said it. First, the room where it happened.

The trial opened on November 20, 1945, in the Palace of Justice at Nuremberg, a German city left in ruins. Twenty-one defendants sat in the dock. Judges from four Allied nations sat above them, and headphones carried four languages.
In the front row sat Wilhelm Keitel, age 63, a Field Marshal in a plain uniform stripped of its insignia. He had been chief of the High Command of the Armed Forces, known as the OKW, since 1938.

Keitel took the witness stand in early April 1946. He spoke as a professional soldier. Prosecutors had piles of documents, many carrying his signature or initials. They wanted to know who made the decisions behind them.

To understand the answer, go back to August 23, 1939. Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact in Moscow. Nine days later Germany invaded Poland. For almost two years, the two dictatorships stayed officially at peace.

Then came the fall of France in June 1940. Germany dominated western Europe, but Britain kept fighting. Hitler began to look east. On July 31, 1940, he told his senior commanders that Russia must be destroyed.

The source for that meeting is the diary of General Franz Halder, the army chief of staff. Halder's notes record that Hitler wanted the attack launched in the spring of 1941. It was written years before any trial.

Planning moved forward. On December 18, 1940, Hitler signed Directive 21, code-named Case Barbarossa. It ordered the armed forces to be ready to crush Soviet Russia in a rapid campaign, even before ending the war against Britain.
The directive was issued by the OKW, Keitel's own headquarters. Copies were numbered and distributed to a short list of senior commanders. Few people knew the full plan. Keitel was one of them.

At Nuremberg, that fact mattered. Keitel was not a stranger to the decision. His office had prepared the paper, carried it, and sent it down the chain of command. So how would he describe his own part?

Keitel's position was simple. In testimony he said the decision belonged to Hitler alone. He portrayed himself as a soldier who obeyed and passed orders along. The answer was short, and it was not entirely false.
That was partly true. Hitler did decide. He held the supreme command himself. Generals did not vote on war. Keitel also testified that he had raised objections to Hitler about an attack on Russia.

But the prosecution did not accept the idea that obeying Hitler removed all responsibility. Under the Nuremberg Charter, acting on orders was not a defense. It could only be considered when judges decided the punishment.

Barbarossa was not planned as an ordinary campaign. Before the invasion, orders went out that treated the war as a struggle of annihilation. Keitel's headquarters issued several of them. The prosecution presented them as evidence.

On May 13, 1941, Keitel signed a decree that limited the prosecution of German soldiers for crimes against Soviet civilians. Such offenses would no longer be punished as a rule. The decree invited abuse of the civilian population.

On June 6, 1941, the OKW issued the Commissar Order. Captured Soviet political officers were to be shot. It violated the laws of war, and it went out under Keitel's authority. The prosecution quoted it line by line.

In the early hours of June 22, 1941, the invasion began. About three million German soldiers, with allied troops, attacked along a front stretching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. It was the largest land invasion in history.

Stalin's armies were taken by surprise, despite warnings. German forces advanced hundreds of miles in weeks, and captured vast numbers of Soviet soldiers. By the end of 1941 the advance stalled outside Moscow in the winter cold.

The war that followed lasted nearly four years. The Soviet Union lost an estimated 27 million people, soldiers and civilians. Millions of Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity. Those figures stood behind every question at Nuremberg.

Soviet prosecutors were in the courtroom, and they pressed hard. They had Keitel's own documents. They had his signature. They wanted him to say plainly whether he had taken part in preparing a war of aggression.

Keitel did not deny the documents. He confirmed his signature again and again. He said he had acted as a soldier under orders. And on the question of who stood behind Barbarossa, he pointed to one man.

That man was Adolf Hitler. Hitler had been dead since April 30, 1945, and he could not answer. The generals and ministers in the dock could say what they wished about a man who could not contradict them.
The judges knew this. They did not simply accept a dead man as the only author. They weighed the papers. They looked at who drafted, who signed, who passed on the orders, and who carried them out.
This mattered because Nuremberg was building a new principle. A leader's order did not erase the guilt of those who helped carry it out. The tribunal was setting a precedent in international law.

For Keitel, the trap was clear. If obedience were enough, nobody would be responsible for anything. Hitler would carry all of it, and the machinery beneath him would carry none. The judges rejected that idea.
In writings from his cell, he admitted that his sense of a soldier's duty had been abused by Hitler. He saw it too late. That was not a defense. It was an admission that his obedience had failed.

The verdict came on October 1, 1946. Keitel was found guilty on all four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The judgment found he had been a willing participant in these crimes.
Keitel asked for one thing. He requested death by firing squad, as a soldier. The court did not grant it. He was sentenced to hang, the same fate as the civilian leaders he had served.

In the early hours of October 16, 1946, Keitel was hanged in the gymnasium of the Nuremberg prison. He was the first of the ten men executed that night. His last words referred to German soldiers who had died.

The consequence outlived him. In December 1946 the United Nations General Assembly affirmed the principles used at Nuremberg. Following orders is not, by itself, a shield against responsibility for crimes under international law.

Nuremberg also left a record. Thousands of captured German documents were entered into evidence, and historians still use them. They show how an order passed from the dictator through a headquarters to the front.
So the short answer was true, and it was not enough. Hitler decided. But Keitel's office drafted, signed, and forwarded the orders that made Barbarossa possible. The court held both facts at once.

Consider what that means. Large wars are not started by one man alone. They need staff officers, clerks, signatures and obedience at every level. Nuremberg asked those people a question, and for Keitel the answer was a single name.
The name was Hitler. The ruling was that it did not excuse the man who said it. Responsibility, the judges held, does not simply stop at the top of the chain of command.

descrizione:
At Nuremberg in 1946, Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel was asked who ordered Operation Barbarossa, the German invasion of the Soviet Union. His answer pointed to one man. This documentary follows the evidence: Directive 21, the Commissar Order, the jurisdiction decree of May 1941, and the testimony heard by the International Military Tribunal.

We trace the road from the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 to the invasion of June 22, 1941, and show why the tribunal rejected the defense of superior orders. You will see how Keitel's verdict, sentence and execution on October 16, 1946 shaped international law.

All scenes use real archival film from the 1930s and 1940s, and every fact comes from documented records and trial testimony.
